utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume our work. Does everybody hear? Do the interpreters hear? Good morning. Mr. Cayley, I see, is here. The Defence is here. Everyone hears. All right. It's 10.00 now. In principle, we will start every day now at a quarter to ten, but, of course, there may be some slight delays here and there for technical reasons or for some other reasons. Good morning, Mr. Cayley, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel. The next witness is a protected witness, Witness UU. He will be giving evidence in closed session. I've spoken with Mr. Nobilo. He is in agreement with this. That is because there is no capacity in this courtroom yet to have a device which distorts the voice to make the voice unrecognisable. The summary, in respect of the witness: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt. This is still a public hearing. Perhaps we should have a closed session for your resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That would be more secure. There are few specific, identifying features in my summary but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dubuisson. Yes, all right, we will have a closed session with the agreement of the Defence, of course. Thank you. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next witness is a Bosnian Muslim who was a former member of the Bosnian army. He belonged to a unit of that army that was stationed near Mostar along the confrontation lines with the Serbs. He will testify that fighting between the HVO and the Muslims occurred in Mostar in May of 1993, and he will testify further that on the 13th of June, 1993, the HVO ordered that his unit be disbanded, and there was some resistance to this order by the HVO. The HVO then threatened to kill members of the families of those people who failed to surrender. As a result of that threat, he and other members of his family surrendered to the HVO. This witness remained a captive of the HVO from the 13th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Harmon. Could you repeat what you just said? The dismembering or the dismantling of the unit. Was that the HVO who asked that the unit be dismantled, of the Bosnian army? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The HVO asked that the unit be disarmed. Now, this witness, Mr. President, remained captured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From the 13th of June, 1993 until the 22nd or 23rd of March of 1994. During this period, he and thousands of civilians, and as well as some prisoners of war, and he technically was a prisoner of war, were incarcerated in the Heliodrom located near Mostar. His testimony will relate primarily to his nine months in captivity at the Heliodrom. He will describe the systematic forced labour of civilians and prisoners of war, including trench digging at front-line positions that resulted in numerous deaths and injuries of detainees. He will also describe the presence of Croatian military units that he observed in and around Mostar, including the First Guards Brigade from Zagreb, they were known as the Tigers and the Second Guards Brigade from Zagreb known as the Thunderbolts. He will testify that he was force to do a number of things, including forced labour in the presence of and at the request of these particular HV units, these Croatian units. He will testify further that he observed these Croatian army units engaged in combat with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Lastly, Mr. President, he will describe how he and other prisoners, including civilians, were used as human shields. Now, in respect of the indictment, Mr. President, his testimony is relevant to show that certain acts in the indictment were widespread and systematic, and this is relevant to crimes against humanity, specifically paragraph 5.2 of the indictment and Count 1 of the indictment. His testimony is also relevant to the existence of an international armed conflict between two sovereign states, Croatia and Bosnia, and this, therefore, is relevant to paragraphs 5.0, 5.1, and 5.3 of the indictment and to all alleged violations of the Geneva Conventions that are contained in counts 5, 8, 11, 15, 17 and 19. That concludes my summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. As I did with Mr. Cayley, I would like to congratulate him for his concision, he's not here but you can congratulate him for me. If I understand you correctly, the witness spent several months in captivity. I would ask you, Mr. Harmon, to concentrate your questions on the three points which seem to be the most important to us, subject to, of course, what the witness will say, that is, the captivity, the engagement of the Croatian army and the human shields. Try to focus on those points. Of course, if you feel there are other important points, don't hesitate to ask questions about them. But, according to your summary, these are the three points which seem to be what you expect the witness to speak about. All right, we can have Witness VV brought in now. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness VV, do you hear me? We're going to call you Witness VV. You are under protection measures. First identify your name on the document that the usher is going to show you. Is this, in fact, your name? Is that your name? Don't say it, just tell us whether that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Remain standing for a few more moments, as long as it takes to take the solemn declaration. You are going to read the document which is the usher is giving to you here. Please read it out loud in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Please get comfortable. Relax. We're going to call you Witness VV because you are a protected witness, at your request and with the agreement of all the parties. You have agreed to come to testify at the request of the Prosecutor. We have a general idea about what the Prosecutor expects from your testimony. You are going to answer a few of his questions, and to say very simply to us what you experienced. Mr. Harmon is going to ask you first some questions and then you will testify freely using your own words before the Judges. Please settle in, relax, feel comfortable. Mr. Harmon? Witness VV

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness VV.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Bosnian citizen and a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In June of 1993, were you a member of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the approximate month when the fighting started between the HVO and the Muslims in the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you taken prisoner by the HVO in June of 1993 and did you remain in captivity until approximately the 22nd or 23rd of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, before we start your testimony, if I could have the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have Prosecutor's Exhibit 401 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel, Your Honours, 401 is -- I'll describe this. This is a map on which Witness VV has indicated and marked certain locations that will be relevant to his testimony. And this is really an aid to Your Honours when he refers to certain locations, Your Honours can refer and counsel can refer to those locations that have been mapped -- marked on the map. Now, let me have this exhibit placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness VV, can you just take a look at that and tell the Judges whether these marks are marks that you indicated and then I subsequently marked on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you testified today, Witness VV, I'd like you to tell your story in your own words in a narrative form to the Judges. And let me begin, if I can, by asking you to tell the Judges about the unit of the Bosnian army in which you were a member, where they were stationed, and the circumstances of your becoming a prisoner of war. Could you tell the Judges in your own words the answers to those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My unit was located in Rotilja. It's a place on the border of Stolac and Mostar. We held positions against Serb units. We were together with the HVO units. To the left and to the right of our position were HVO positions, also facing the Serb units. After the fighting broke out in Mostar on the 13th of June, those HVO units were reinforced and they were under the orders to disarm our unit. After a brief fighting of a platoon, a part of the unit was able to retreat to Mostar and to connect linkup with the Mostar units. And the other part of the unit remained blocked there, surrounded. And after the threats of the HVO soldiers that they would kill our families located on certain buses, it turned out that it was not true that they were on those buses, that part of the unit surrendered. I was among them. The very same day, we were taken to the prison in Gabela, and then on the same day to the Heliodrom prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, just very briefly, what was your role in the Bosnian army? What was your position? What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit had just been founded, and formal appointments were not made. I was in charge of four or five men who were in charge of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell the Judges where you were held prisoner and the conditions of your captivity, and while describing those experiences, what happened to you and what happened to other people who were prisoners, can you also describe your contacts with members of the Croatian army and Croatian army units? Just start at the beginning, then, once you were taken prisoner and carry us all the way through the time of your release, if you would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Before the witness begins to tell the story of his captivity, rather than interrupt him in the middle of his description, we're going to take a 20-minute break. We will now adjourn the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon and Witness VV, you may now proceed with the account of your captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness VV, before we left, the question I had asked you is if you could kindly tell the Judges of the conditions under which you were held a prisoner, where you were held prisoner, relate those experiences and the experiences of others, if you would. Would you kindly also describe to the Judges your contacts with soldiers from the Croatian army and, particularly, identify Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after the capture, we were taken to Gabela, that was a former depot of the Yugoslav People's Army, and we were kept there for several hours. After those several hours, we were transported to the Heliodrom. The "Heliodrom" is the term used for centre which was -- actually, it was a school for airmen, air personnel, in the former Yugoslav People's Army. There were lots of buildings. There was a gym there. One of the buildings became a prison, and we called that building the prison. And that's where we were located, in the basement in that building, and that's where we remained for 20 days. A little while later, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina managed to break through towards the north and they managed to liberate the area of Bijelo Polje and Sjeverni Logor, northern camp. Immediately after that in our prison, in the gym and the buildings, civilians from Mostar were brought to those rooms. A few days later, we started to work. I spent about nine months in the Heliodrom. Various trucks of various HVO units came every day, and they took prisoners, as many as they needed for the works, took them to the location where they were supposed to do the labour, and that was at the HVO positions. In the evening, most often they would return them to the prison, although there were cases when we would stay several days or even several weeks at the positions of those units. Since we were young and strong during the nine months, we worked virtually every day. The jobs what we did were various. At the frontlines, we would carry sacks with sand or dug trenches or unload the ammunition. And we also loaded and unloaded timber, that was in the rear. The first contact with the soldiers of the Croatian army occurred approximately in August 1993 in the village of Bijelo Polje. The HVO took a group of prisoners, including myself, to Bijelo Polje and that's where we stayed for seven days. On one of those seven days, I was digging side trenches on the position next to the main route, the Sarajevo-Mostar main route. That location on that day was held by a platoon strength unit of the Croatian army. I don't know what unit of the Croatian army those soldiers belonged to, but they talked to us, since they were from Slavonia. They were soldiers of the Croatian army. And during the fighting with the Yugoslav People's Army in Slavonia, they were captured as members of the Croatian army. And then when they were exchanged and brought back to Croatia, they again joined the Croatian army, and it was interesting for them to compare their experience as prisoners of war with our experience. On that day, there was sporadic exchange of infantry weapons fire. And the next encounter was on the hill of Kicin near Blagaj. It was approximately in September or maybe early October 1993. Since there were no roads on that hill, we were forced to carry crates with infantry ammunition to the top of that hill. These positions were also held by the units of the Croatian army. I don't know what unit that was. We went there a couple of times. Actually, I climbed three times up that hill carrying a load of about 30 kilos. The soldiers of that unit told us that on that day, an officer of the Croatian army who was doing artillery reconnaissance, that he was captured by the BH army. Approximately seven days after that, we were taken to a mortar position held by the Croatian army. That was the Second Guards Brigade, Thunder Bolts. That was a mortar position in placement 72 and 120 millimetres -- 82 millimetres, I apologise. I went five or six times to that position during the next 10 or 20 days. They would take us there every time from the Heliodrom prison and bring us back the same day after we carried out our tasks. During the last three months of my detention in the prison, I worked in the Heliodrom compound in the rooms occupied by the members of the Croatian army unit of Tigrovi, that's the Tigers, the First Guards Brigade from Zagreb. While I was there, I mostly worked in the kitchen or I was cleaning the pots and so on. In between those events, we worked with the Croatian Defence Council for them almost every day. All those tasks involved great risks working at the front-line, and prisoners were often wounded. During the first days of my detention in Heliodrom, we went to work -- it was only us members of the BH army who went to work in those early days. Our uniforms of the BH army, we had to take them off, and we were given old blue former JNA uniforms. And we were, thus, marked as members of the BH army so that it was easy to notice us, even when we were working in the town, when there was street fighting going on. However, when civilians were brought into the prison, since the number of imprisoned soldiers was small and they had great needs to have people to work, everybody went to work. When we were building bunkers in abandoned apartments in the town where the street fighting was going on, we found certain items of clothing, shirts and trousers. And over the next month or so, we managed to change from those uniforms gradually, and we blended into that mass of civilians. So from the second month onwards, there was no difference in our status of us prisoners of war, members of the BH army, and the civilians. In March 1993, I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said just a moment ago in March of 1993, you were exchanged. Did you mean March of 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, it was March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness VV, before I turn to a different subject, let me just ask some questions to clarify some of your testimony. Do you see in front of you Prosecutor's Exhibit 401? You have mentioned the Heliodrom. Is the location of the Heliodrom indicated, marked in orange, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 401, and could you point to it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the area that is marked on the map at Jesenica. This is in the southern part of Mostar. On the right side of Neretva, the river Neretva, and there was the barracks Heliodrom. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges approximately how many prisoners you estimate were present at the Heliodrom during your nine-month stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We prisoners, we thought that there were between 3.000 and 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, how many of those prisoners were prisoners of war and how many of them were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly a hundred prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the remainder of the prisoners, in your opinion, civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least a hundred people were captured in the uniforms of the BH army. The others were civilians, among them also people who were able to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell me, were the people who were prisoners detained with you and others Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were mostly Muslims. There were also two Serbs that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there women detained as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the last floor, there were a few women.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the range in ages of the men who were detained at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were men aged 16 to 17 to over 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you described being taken to dig trenches. Were you and the others taken to, not only front-line positions, but positions within the city of Mostar where fighting was occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I say "lines, frontlines," I mean Mostar and the surrounding because this line was very broad. There were street fights in Mostar, and it was most dangerous to work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn your attention to the area that is marked on the map in pen, Bijelo Polje. You described first coming into contact at that location with members of the Croatian army. Can you tell the Judges, were they wearing uniforms that indicated they were members of the Croatian army? Were they wearing insignia that indicated that they were members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember regarding this unit, the insignia exactly, but I can remember the conversation we had with them where they confirmed that they are members of HV, especially their experience with regard to their capture in Slavonia and exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at this particular location, how far away were you and the other prisoners from the frontlines with the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 100 and 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were at that particular location, did the members of the Croatian army engage in fighting with members of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was some exchange of infantry shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn your attention to the second location where you observed Croatian soldiers, that is, the area marked on the map as "Blagaj." I'd like to ask you some specific questions about that particular unit. Did that unit of Croatian soldiers appear to be an organised unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with their command and with their complete unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they wearing some kind of an insignia that indicated that they were from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to these soldiers, I don't remember that they had any insignia. I remember that an officer visited them and he had an insignia of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember what that insignia was or did you later see that officer in another location and then did you know what unit he was a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on when I worked in the kitchen with the unit, the Tigers, I saw that this officer is their superior and that he is a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this particular officer you remember visiting the unit, the Croatian unit, that was stationed at Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they were located at the positions towards Blagaj. Blagaj is a place that was under the control of the BH army and this is the hill Kicin near Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, just a second, the unit, the Tigers, is a Croatian unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I see an error that I've made, Judge Riad. Let's just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Tigers, that was a unit of the Croatian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tigers, yes, it's the First Guards Brigade of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn your attention to Hodbina, and that is an area that is also marked on Prosecutor's Exhibit 401, and that is the third location where you saw soldiers from the Croatian army. Just to clarify one point, you said these were the Second Guards unit known as the Thunder Bolts. Do you know from which city the Thunder Bolts came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Thunder Bolts are, as far as I know, the Second Guards Brigade from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in the presence of the Thunder Bolts, what kind of work did you do? What kind of work were you forced to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were cleaning the mortars. We were bringing the munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you personally observe the members of the Croatian army, the Thunder Bolts, fire on Bosnian army positions with those mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two times I was there when they were shooting from the -- when there was mortar shooting from these positions towards the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see the impacts of those mortar rounds on Bosnian frontlines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could see that -- I could see that one house was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you had returned to the Heliodrom, and then in the morning you would be picked up and brought back to various positions, including this position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the vehicle which transported you from the Heliodrom to this particular Croatian army position near Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were vehicles that belonged to the JNA, former JNA, normal trucks. They had shields of the Croatian army -- number plates of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did the soldiers who you saw, who were members of the Thunder Bolts, also have Croatian army insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had the insignia of the Thunder Bolts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to the fourth time you were in the presence of Croatian army soldiers, and you testified that that was when you worked in the kitchen at the Heliodrom. And you worked in the presence of the first guards brigade known as the Tigers who was also from Zagreb. Let me ask you some questions. Did this unit appear to be an organised unit, functioning as an organised unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Completely organised unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were in their presence for three months, approximately; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately three months. Every morning I went to work there, and every evening I went back to the prison to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Witness VV, did members of the Tigers engage in combat against Bosnian army units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw that. I heard that the Major of their army, of the Tigers, explain what an important role the Tigers had as an intervening unit at stopping the BH army in taking the hill Hum which was close to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you had the opportunity to hear the Croatian soldiers talking about combat activities that they had engaged in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about those activities regarding the hill Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, you've described being taken, you being taken, to various front-line positions and engaged in forced labour, and civilians also having to engage in that same kind of labour. Were you aware of any prisoners of war and civilians who were killed or wounded as a result of being placed in those dangerous situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there when some civilians were wounded and killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, where is "there"? Can you just describe in your own words what you saw, who took you there, what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the worst cases that I saw was in the street Santic in Mostar. That is a street where the street fighting was heaviest or worst. It happened very often that the positions of the HVO and Bosnia and Herzegovina were in the same building. One day, the HVO units took us to work there, me and another four prisoners, and they forced us to push a wreck of a car to a cellar window for building where there were the positions of the BH army. The distance from us and this window was about 15 metres, and the wreck of the car had no motor, so that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, could the witness repeat the sentence? We had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very clear to us that we could do nothing about it, that this was a very difficult task. At that moment, the HVO soldiers were shooting above our heads, and they were threatening that they would kill us if we don't do it. We tried to turn the car for the first time, and the BH army started shooting at us from their bunker. One prisoner was dead immediately, and two were heavily wounded. One of those seriously wounded was a civilian. I know that for sure because he was sleeping in my room. And the second one who was wounded and killed, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said that he was in your room. How many people, how many other prisoners, were in your room? And out of that number, how many were killed or injured as a result of being shot for their activities at the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the room where I was, there were 80 to 100 people. Now I can remember four or five of them that were wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges as well about a time that there was a human shield event that took place near the village of Rastani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In autumn '93, BH army took over the place Rastani. It is actually the northern suburb of Mostar. Immediately, the day after, the HVO units tried to take that again. In these fights, they had wounded and dead people. The side from which they were trying to conquer, Rastani, was a very difficult one. They couldn't carry out all of their wounded and dead. So they prepared a group of prisoners, I was among them as well, and they had to go towards the place where the fighting was. And our movement was controlled from the positions above us. When we came close to the line, we saw or met two groups of HVO soldiers who divided our group into two groups. They lined us up, four next to each other, and then they forced us as a human shield to move towards the area where they could look for a secure shelter or position for themselves. During that movement, they were completely hiding behind our bodies. From my group, no one was wounded or killed on that occasion. From the second group, some prisoners were declared later on missing. For some of them, we don't know even today what their fate was. And some managed to run over to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Lastly, Witness VV, you spent nine months in captivity. How much weight did you lose as a result of remaining in captivity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was captured, I weighed about 90 kilograms, and when I left, I had 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions of Witness VV. I would move to admit Prosecutor's Exhibit 401 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. No comments from the Defence? Witness VV, you are now going to be asked some questions by General Blaskic's Defence counsel. General Blaskic is the accused in this courtroom here today. Mr. Nobilo, you can begin now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness VV. You said that you were a member of the BH army. Can you please tell me, is it true that your unit was seconded or attached to the HVO in that particular sector or area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly that that was the case. At that part of the front, it is true that at that part of the front, the position of our unit was established after the HVO didn't allow us to be in Stolac. So after we had several discussions and negotiations, we find such a compromising solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The municipality of Stolac was held by Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness VV, when you hear the questions, please look at Mr. Nobilo who is on your left. But when you answer them, please look at the Judges. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So my next question is whether the municipality of Serbs (sic) was held by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It seems that there is an interpretation error. I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the municipality of Stolac, was it held by Serbs? Was it controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in May, the conflict between the HVO and the BH army broke out in Mostar. And there where you were at the frontlines, the ultimatum for the surrender of weapons and the conflict itself, it all happened a month later; is that correct? So is it true that between May and June, your area was peaceful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no fighting between the BH army and HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that there were threats against soldiers' families. I fail to understand whether this threat was real. What happened later? What did you learn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, we realised that they were not real threats but they had, as a consequence, the surrender of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in the BH army unit, you were in charge of a unit that was working on communications. Can you tell me at what level? Was it battalion, brigade, corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our unit was a brigade, but as far as the numbers are concerned, we couldn't call it a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said, furthermore, that civilians, including women, were transferred to the Heliodrom. Did they stay there for a longer time or were they returned to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were there for a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The civilians who were captured, can you please tell us, could we define them as civilians that were of a military age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So what would be the ages that you would consider as not being eligible to do military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people who were not of full age, and there were also older people who, according to their physical condition, with regard to their age and their physical condition, could not be able to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the offer made by the HVO to people who were detained in Heliodrom, that they can leave the place under the condition that they leave Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that offer accepted by anyone from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some prisoners accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In order to keep things clear, your brigade belonged to the fourth corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you encountered soldiers who talked amongst themselves that they were members of the Tigers, but that you did not see the insignia. Can you please tell me, did they speak about having come there under somebody's orders or did they volunteer? Do you know anything about the way in which they arrived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which meeting you mean. The last month when I worked with the Tigers, I could see their insignia very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I meant the first encounter. But, nevertheless, in the conversations that you had with the Tigers or the Thunder Bolts, did you learn, did they tell you, whether they were volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't conclude by anything that they are volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ask them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the prisoner is not in the position to ask such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You indicated several positions where you dug trenches, and you saw some members of the Croatian army on some of those positions. Can you please tell me, at what distance were Serb positions from those positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position in Hodbina, they were away for about three or four kilometres from these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hodbina is close to Blagaj. The Croatian army could not hold the positions in Blagaj because Blagaj was kept by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the nearest Serb position to Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before you were captured, while you were still together with the HVO holding the front-line against the Serbs, did you see Croatian soldiers or officers there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How much do you weigh now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ninety-three kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, have you any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness VV.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions just to make things clearer in my mind. You spoke about the Thunder Bolts. This is a Croatian brigade or a Bosnian Croatian brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a brigade of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Completely. And you said that they were shooting on the Bosnian army positions. Where were they shooting from? Was it from Croatia or were they inside Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you spoke also of the Tigers whom you saw when you were working in the kitchen. Where was that? Was it in Mostar? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the Heliodrom in the barracks which are the southern suburbs of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was HVO barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were HVO barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the Tigers were Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is a unit of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there were units from the HVO and the Croatian army together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, within the area of these barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned also that you heard that the Tigers prevented the HV army from taking the hill Hum. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hill Hum is a hill that dominates Mostar. Actually, the lobes of that hill are actually the centre of Mostar almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you say "the Tigers," it means the Croatian unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the Croatian army units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The Croatian army unit. You also mentioned that the soldiers had to hide behind the bodies of the prisoners to reach a secure area and to use you as human shields. What soldiers were they? Were they Croatian or were they HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They were HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Finally, you lost something like 20 kilograms. You said you lost from 90 to 72 kilograms in captivity. Were the conditions so bad? Did you have food? Why did you lose such weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't really starve. I think I lost so much weight because I was working so much every day, physically working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any beating, any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times, I got a few blows, but other prisoners were not that lucky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They had more than that. What did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My colleague had to hold his hands on his head and close his eyes, sitting on the earth, while a group of soldiers was torturing him, beating him. He was completely blue afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness VV. I myself have no questions. The Tribunal thanks you for your testimony. You may now go back to your home, if you still have a home. We can ask the usher to accompany Witness VV out of the courtroom, thank you, and then we will hear the programme for the rest of the day. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have two additional witnesses for today, but I did think that we would go to lunch with the two that we had. And I think we can start earlier after lunch, because I'll get the witnesses here, but I have two more witnesses. We will get through them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you never have faith in your own synthesising efforts, you see. You are a synthetic type person and you move more quickly than you believe you can. You just don't believe in your own skills which means we don't have any witnesses right now. Very well. Then we are going to adjourn, that will be fine for the interpreters, who often do a bit more than they really have to, so that will be a good thing. We will resume at 2.30. And we will conclude our work on Friday in the late morning. You were able to carry out your examination the way you wanted to, but getting to the essential, and I ask that you continue in that same way. I ask the same thing of the Defence which tried to concentrate its questions in relation to the examination-in-chief. Having made this congratulations and having thanked the interpreters, I repeat that we will resume at 2.30. The hearing is now adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.23 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please, General Blaskic? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you will be the one who is conducting the questioning now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. Mr. President, good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next witness that we have is a non-protected witness. He will have no protections at all. He will be talking about an area in and around Mostar, and if I could highlight the ELMO just briefly, this is Exhibit 306 that the court has. And as the court notes, there is a Mostar highlighted in green. That's fine, Mr. Usher, if we can. And going just left -- down and left of Mostar is a town called Rodoc. Rodoc is the area that Your Honours heard described this morning as the Heliodrom. The Heliodrom is located in Rodoc. That's very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How are you pronouncing it? I see Rodoc. How do you say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we continue to move left and down of Rodoc, there's a town called Citluk. That is another location that we will be talking about. The witness that you are about to here, Mr. President, Your Honours, his name is Dragan Becirovic. At the time of the events that he will describe to you, he was about 14 years old, he and his twin brother. And they will discuss some events that took place just prior to the outbreak of hostilities between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which commenced on the 9th of May of 1993. He will talk to you about the presence of forces from the Republic of Croatia known in the terminology and the parlance before this court as HV troops. He will talk to you about having seen HV soldiers in cafes, the HV soldiers in the Heliodrom, HV plates on automobiles and trucks moving throughout the Mostar area. And then he will discuss with the court the events after the outbreak of hostilities on the 9th of May, 1993, the arrest of Bosnian Muslims, several thousand, estimates to 8.000 to 9.000 arrested, their incarceration in various camps, including the Heliodrom in and around the Mostar area. He will then talk about the blockade that existed in and around Mostar between the 9th of May, 1993 and the 30th of June, 1993. And then he will talk about what happened after the 30th of June, 1993 when the cleansing of Bosnian Muslims from West Mostar commenced in earnest and how the HVO -- initially, the HVO military police went house to house rounding up men and taking them from their various homes and flats in the Mostar area. During one of these encounters on the 30th of May, at approximately 5.00 p.m., his father was taken out. Thereafter that evening, about 10.00 in the evening of the 30th of June, and I think it's interesting to note just ironically, if nothing else, that it's five years to the day of this event, the HV military police, not the HVO, the military police of the Republic of Croatia came back to his flat and took his oldest brother, his mother, Dragan, and his twin, Goran, out, placed them in a vehicle, and took them to a garbage dump in the area of Citluk and, at that point, commenced to execute them at point-blank range, maybe not point-blank range, but at several metres distance. His mother was executed by these HV troops. His brother was executed by these HV troops, and his brother Goran was severely wounded and Dragan, while wounded as well, was able to pull himself out of a garbage dump heap and tried to get some help, which he did. He will explain to you exactly what had -- how he got that help and how his brother's life was saved by being brought to a hospital in Mostar. He will then talk about the continued -- or visits by HV troops to him once they had learned that the two twins, Goran and Dragan, were still -- or hadn't been killed on the night of the 30th. And interestingly, there is a visit from a SIS colonel or a Secret Service colonel in the service of the Republic of Croatia who comes to the hospital to ask questions of these particular boys. In addition to those particular matters, he will talk about the prisoners that were brought in to this hospital over the course of time he was there. As the witness this morning noted, the witness noted a street in Mostar called Santic street, which was a dangerous street on the front-line, where various Bosnian Muslims were taken to work and shot. These two boys were back in the hospital recovering from those wounds when these Bosnian Muslims who had been taken to the camps and then taken out to dig in Santic Street were brought in with their wounds. He will talk about some discussions with some of these individuals that had been brought from as far away as Maglaj and had been taken out to dig trenches not only in Mostar but also for various HV positions. He will talk about the existence of the Tigers, an HV unit that was discussed this morning, and the participation of the Tigers in a retaking of a feature called Hum, as Your Honours heard this morning, which had been attacked by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Tigers, this HV unit, assisted in the retaking of that feature. Lastly, he will talk about the actual leaving of Mostar, their escape from Mostar through Zagreb with the assistance of UNHCR, and then their ultimate departure through a third country. The evidence to be addressed by this witness will focus on various counts in the indictment. As my colleague, Mr. Harmon, mentioned this morning with the other witness, the charges in Count 1 encompass a persecution charge which envisages of proving of widespread and systematic persecution of the Bosnian Muslim population. His testimony will go to the persecution charge as far as this widespread and systematic persecution of the Bosnian Muslim population as set forth in Count 1. Likewise, as my colleague, Mr. Harmon, mentioned this morning, the article 2 charges set forth in the indictment require approving of an international armed conflict. The evidence presented by this witness concerning the participation of HV troops, troops belonging to the Republic of Croatia, is further evidence of the internationality of this conflict or the fact that it was an international armed conflict. So, Mr. President and Your Honours, that is the basic outline of the witness's testimony and the particular counts in the indictment that his evidence will address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. I've checked on the problem about the oath. He is a Major now, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he was 14 at the time, so that was five years ago, Mr. President. I believe that he is over the age of majority, assuming the age of majority is 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. This is the question that I'm asking to know, what is the age that one has -- the legal age? What are the general provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As regards to the age of the witnesses, I do not think that it is specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, it's in Rule 90. In Rule 90, it says that a child can testify, but it doesn't actually say anything in particular about this. In the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Nobilo, what is the age when one becomes -- what is the legal age?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 18 years of age, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How old is he now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, he is 19, maybe 20 years of age, something in that range. He's over 18 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. All right. He will take an oath under normal conditions. I just wanted to check on this point. We can now have the witness brought in. This is an open session. This is Dragan Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have your headset on. You are Mr. Dragan Becirovic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How old are you, please, and what is your profession? How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm 20 years and I'm a student.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before you sit down, you are going to read the solemn declaration which is the oath that you have to take before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. You have come here at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor to testify for the Prosecution as part of the trial before the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, the trial of General Blaskic, the accused who is sitting here in this courtroom. Speak without fear, without hatred about the difficult events that you experienced. If you need to take a break, please don't hesitate to ask for some time. You'll make your -- give your testimony freely. The Prosecutor has explained generally to us what you're going to speak about, but be free to say what you want, to say in your own words and according to your own sensitivities about these events. The Prosecutor will ask you several questions, and after that, you will testify -- after that, you know or you must have been told, the Defence attorneys will also most likely ask you some questions within the scope of the cross-examination, and the Judges will also have some questions to ask you. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dragan Becirovic

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Becirovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you just told the court that you are 20 years of age; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you are a Bosnian Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of the war in May of 1993, you lived in Mostar with your father and your mother, your older brother and your twin Goran; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, can you tell the court in your own words what happened to you and your family in Mostar shortly before the outbreak of hostilities where you observed HV troops in the area. What happened when the hostilities broke out on the 9th of May through the 30th of June, and then what happened on the 30th of June and thereafter until you left the city of Mostar in September of 1993? Could you do that in your own words? Just look at the Judges and tell them that story.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. On the 9th of May, an attack by the Croatian units occurred against the units of the Bosnian army. That was in the morning. I was, at the time, with my family in our apartment. The attack began around 5.00 a.m., and around 9.00, the Muslim population, that is, the Bosniaks started to be picked up from their apartments and they were all taken to the stadium. And from there, they were taken to the Heliodrom camp. Our apartment, our building was protected by a person whose name I don't know, so that nobody was taken out from our building, but from other buildings, and that was all over Mostar, over 8.000 people were taken out. Later on, when Croats, the Croatian units, realised that even the sick people were taken away, during the next two or three days, they started to release those people of whom they had no evidence that they belonged to the BH army or that they had resisted the Croatian forces in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to interrupt. Could the witness clarify whether he means Croatian units or HVO, if he knows the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was going to ask him the same question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you understand what Judge Riad asked you, if you can make a distinction between HVO troops and HV troops to the extent that you know the distinction. And when you're giving your narrative, if you could make that distinction, I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the attack was carried out by the HVO. That was from the western side of the river against the BH army forces located in the city centre. This is where the command of the BH army was located. After this command fell, the attack spread to the whole of the city of Mostar, and then lines were set up and sniper shooting began, so that many people who did not know those frontlines were set up, when they crossed from the left side to the right side, they were fired on by snipers and many people were killed in this manner. These were mostly Croats who were unaware of that fact. So that was an absurd situation. Later on -- so this attack was carried out by HVO troops. Since they saw within the next two or three days that they could not take Mostar without suffering large casualties and that they needed more forces, then they adopted new tactics. The eastern part of Mostar, which was controlled by the BH army, was blocked, and that was a form of pressure. They wanted to pressurise them into surrendering themselves without any casualties. Later on, they picked up Muslim population from the western part of the town which was controlled by them. They gathered them all in camps, and then they separated them in categories according to their own criteria which they set up themselves, whether somebody would be sent to prison, that is, members of the BH army went to the military prison, and the rest of the civilian population was placed in hangars located in the Heliodrom compound. As I said, during the next few days, some people were released. People who were sick, who required medical treatment, they were released to go back to their homes, into the city. And later on, under pressure of the international community and other factors, they slowly started to release the rest of the population. I can't tell you what the number was, but I can give you an approximation, about 7.000 people were released out of the 8.000. In those days, my family was in a state of complete confusion. All of a sudden, we had to hide the fact that we were Muslim because we would be in trouble otherwise. You can compare that to the Jews under the Third Reich. So we continued to go to school, my twin and myself. We had to speak Croatian language because there are differences between Croatian language and the language that I speak, my language, so as not to be discovered. And this situation went on until the 30th of June. This is when members of the military police arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, let me stop you before you start talking about the 30th of June. You said that you had to hide the fact that you were a Muslim. Tell the Judges why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We had to hide that fact, because if you were to show the fact that you were a Muslim, anyone could kill you right there on the spot, and he would not be responsible to anyone. He would not be prosecuted before any court. At that time, they had the free hand. They could do whatever they wanted to. The police did not function. The police functioned superficially, but it wasn't functioning in any real way. For instance, they came to our apartment on one occasion to take away our car, and they said that they needed it. And when the police came, and when they met those people who were about to take our property away, the car, I mean, they did nothing. This is just proof that the police did not function. And then later on, this situation with the Muslims became untenable. It was impossible to live like that anymore. You can't just keep hiding all the time. You can really compare that to the situation with the Jews. I can't really describe it. However, there was no mistreatment, but one had to hide. Later on in the middle of that period, from the 9th of May until the 30th of June, two military police officers came to a person, since they found out that that person was a member of the BH army military police, and they learned from him that my older brother, who was a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, ministry of the interior, and he worked at the old bridge. He worked there as an interpreter. He led the journalists around the town. He explained to them what the town looked like and so on. He got that job through my mother who was a MUP inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. This was another one of your brothers? I'm not sure I caught that. Excuse me. Your twin brother or was it an older brother? I have a translator saying elder brother.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, my older brother, since my twin brother was 14 at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you had another brother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother had to join the armed forces because people who were not mobilised were taken directly to the frontlines. And since my mother worked in the ministry of the interior, she was able to find him a job in the rear so as to avoid any possibility, any danger of his getting killed, since it was really much more difficult to be at the frontlines. So my brother found a job as an interpreter with the ministry of the interior at the checkpoint at the old bridge. So to go back to my story, that person who said that my brother belonged to the ministry of the interior was arrested, together with my brother. I don't know the exact date, but it was in the middle of that period, between the 9th of May and the 30th of June. On that very same day, my brother was arrested and taken to the military police headquarters in Mostar. That was at the faculty there. He was detained there. And since my father had some people that he knew privately, our family friends, who worked in those places, who were members of the Croatian Defence Council military police, he intervened. And since my brother was merely an interpreter, he was not an important person for the military police of the HVO, he was released and he was free to go home. So we come now to the 30th of June. On the 30th of June, the attack of the BH army began on the positions of the HVO in the northern camp. That's in the northern part of Mostar. In order to lift the siege and in order to make communications with Sarajevo, because people who lived in the eastern part of Mostar, they were starving. They knew what hunger was, and they were not able to survive anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me clarify a point. Was East Mostar at this point a predominantly Muslim area of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. All of the city of Mostar had about 70 per cent Bosniaks and Muslims, and the rest, the surrounding area was held by Croats. Those villages in the surrounding area, they made it equal, the number of people, the percentages of the population was equal. But in the centre of the city, it was mostly Muslims who lived there. Let me give you an example of my building. Out of 12 families who lived there, two were Croat families and four Serbian. The rest were all Muslim families. So the city of Mostar itself, the centre of the city, had the majority Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move, if you will, to the events of the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, the army launched the attack, and then later on when some units of the Croatian Defence Council crossed over to the side held by the BH army, the first battalion -- actually, that brigade was responsible for the northern part of Mostar, it had the 70 per cent of Muslims, maybe less, maybe more. Those Muslims voluntarily crossed over to the Bosnian army side, and then they liberated Bijelo Polje later on. That's north of Mostar, and crossed over to the right side. That's the area of Rastane. This all happened within the time period of two or three hours. And then the Croat forces stabilised themselves and started to set up lines, frontlines. And then when the frontlines were stabilised once again, people were gathered again, picked up again. This time it was a selective process, just the Muslim population. If you were older than 16 and younger than 68, you were picked up and taken away. Even if you, for instance, belonged to the Croatian Defence Council units or some other Croatian armed forces units. On the 30th of June, our building was not an exception anymore. They started to pick up people from our building again. They gathered the people who lived there too. Since we knew that my older brother had already been arrested by the military police of the Croatian Defence Council, my father and my mother hid him in the balcony, in a cupboard located in the balcony, in order to avoid another arrest. Because if he would have been arrested again, he probably would not have returned. So the two of us, when I say "the two of us" I mean my twin brother and myself, since we were 14 years of age, we were not taken away. We had our birth certificates, and we showed that to the military policemen who came to our door. And only our father went away with them. Not my father, but the rest of the people were abused, physically or mentally. For instance, some people had their ears cut off. I saw that personally from the window of my building, and so on. People gathered in front of the buildings, and then buses would arrive and then they were taken away to the Heliodrom. As I said already, my father was taken away and the four of us, my mother, my twin brother, my older brother, we remained in the apartment. And on the very same day, the 30th of June, this gathering of people, this all happened in the period from 3.00 to 5.00 in our neighbourhood. And in other neighbourhoods, this action lasted until midnight. Since we're talking about 8.000 people, that's a lot of people to gather in just one day. So that on that very same day, around 10.00 p.m., the four of us, we were all in one room, we heard some noise coming from the area in front of our house. When we looked through the window, we saw four soldiers. We did not see the insignia at that time. Since we were watching them from the sixth floor, we saw them knock or beat at the next door building. Since that building had the number 35, and our building was 35A, they must have made a mistake, thinking that they had the right building. And then they didn't see that there should be a letter A. So they beat on the door, and then a man, I don't know who it was, opened the door on our building and invited them in. They went in and went directly to the sixth floor. This is where we lived. And on the sixth floor, that shows that they had an address. Since they went directly to the sixth floor without stopping anywhere, they weren't looking for names, they knew in advance which floor we lived in. And the three of us, the three brothers, our mother told us to get into the bed and to pretend that we were asleep. And she opened the front door to our apartment. Those four men barged in. We were in the room. When they got in, they did not allow us to switch on the lights. They entered with their own torches and lit their way with them. When they entered our room with their rifles at the ready, they ordered us to get up. When we asked them whether we could switch on the lights, they allowed us to do so. We then realised that these were four young men, aged between 20 and 25, with a crew-cut. They were tall and thin, and they had the insignia of the HV, so HV, not HVO, military police. They had white bands and that indicated that they were the military police of the HV. When they started to talk to us, when they told us to get dressed, I recognised the accent of the city of Split which is different from the Bosnian accent and from any other accent. So that I recognised them, that they were not from Mostar, that they were from the outside. When I mean the accent from Split, I mean the Dalmatian accent, because you can't really say whether they were from Split or somewhere else in Dalmatia. At any rate, they told us to get dressed, and since we pretended that we were asleep, they told us to put on our shoes. Then we had to search the apartment at their behest. They were doing that because they were afraid of some bombs, some explosions, some trip wire or boobytraps, so that we had to take all the clothes out of the cupboards and they were watching us while we did that. They were actually looking for money, for German marks. They asked, "Where are the German marks?" Since we didn't have any money at the time, any German marks, we said, "No, we don't have any." After that, they said, "Put on your shoes and get ready." My mother asked one of those soldiers whether she could take my medication, because I was on medication at the time. She thought that we would be going for questioning, that we would be questioned. And then when we got dressed and went down to the front door to the building, we came to a white van with yellow license plates. These were the license plates of the HV, not HVO, because HVO license plates were white. And on that vehicle, it was written VPHV, that's military police of the Croatian army. And it was -- the sign was made with tapes -- it was taped on. We entered into the vehicle. One of them was with us, and the other three went back to the building. They returned after about 20 minutes. When they returned, they asked the one who stayed with us, who was taking care of us, they asked, "Where shall we take them? Shall we take them to the northern location or to the southern location?" Later on I found out that they actually meant, should we take them to the northern location where there was a mine, where people were also killed, a coal mine, or to the south location, and they decided they would take us to the southern part. Later on, when everyone got into the van, they wanted to go to the faculty where there was the headquarters of their military police of HV. As they didn't know the route to the headquarters of the military police, they asked us. So we were actually the ones who were explaining them, and we were showing them where they have to turn and how to drive. And when we arrived in front of the military police, HV, one of them left the van and I guess he didn't want to be present. He went out and he went towards the building of the faculty where the headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, let me ask you a couple of questions before you move away from the university. You noted that the license plates that you saw on that vehicle were HV military police license plates in yellow; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, I saw it because we were entering from the rear side of the car, and I could exactly see it. And as the colour of the car was white, it was very visible, that the plates were yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, had you seen those types of license plates, yellow HV license plates, in Mostar before the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw different cars with such license plates. They were driving around the western part of Mostar because the Mostars were allowed to walk in these parts. We could walk where we wanted, but not outside the city. And I also saw members of the Croatian army who were freely spending their free time there, I guess, when they weren't at the front-line, they were in Mostar. And they would go to the cafes where we would also go when we were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So during this time frame, you saw HV soldiers in Mostar as well as vehicles with HV license plates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And they were not hiding. They were not hiding that the Croatian army was in Mostar city. That was not a secret at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Dragan, on the 30th, you told the Judges that between 3.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon, your area, in your area, Muslims were being arrested, including your father; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I already mentioned why my brother was not arrested, as he -- my mother and my father were hiding him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during those arrests on the afternoon of the 30th of June, were those arrests done by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was done by the soldiers of the HV military police. They did it that way, that they would first enter first with heavy weapons into the apartments, HV military police. And after them, normal police of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they tried to prevent any kind of, maybe, fighting or resistance in that way, because first came heavy armed forces and then heavy armed HVO forces and then normal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, I think you said in the transcript that HV military police participated in the arrest of your father. Was that HV or HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I haven't understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me attempt to clarify an answer that you gave, Dragan. When your father was arrested on the afternoon of the 30th, was it HVO military police that participated in the arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was arrested by the military police of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were arrested with your family at 10.00 that evening, were those HV military police or HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was military police HV, Croatian army. They spoke with the Dalmatian accent. And it was also proof that they were coming from Croatian and not from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, one last question on this area before we allow you to continue your story. When your father and the other individuals were arrested and put in the buses, were the people that were arrested all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These were all Muslims 16 years of age to 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's continue with your story and I interrupted you at the point where the HV vehicle with these four individuals had come to the HVO police location at University of Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, and further on, that man left, that soldier, he left the car, and we continued our travel to the route towards Citluk outside of Mostar. At several checkpoints that are outside of the city of Mostar, two or three, I don't know the exact number, we were not stopped by the soldiers who were there at that moment on duty. The vehicle would slow down, greet the soldiers that were on duty at that time. I guess they knew each other because they didn't show any documents. They didn't have to prove who they were. They just asked, "How are you doing," and they continued travelling. When we started leaving Mostar, the city itself, we went towards Citluk, Brkanova Birla (phoen), over Brkanova Birla to correct myself. And there's a curve on the road. It's somewhere between Mostar and Citluk and there we turned on a route, a Makadem (phoen) route. Until then, we were not particularly upset because we didn't really know what to expect. We just thought that they would interrogate us. We knew that we were no kind of danger to the Croatian army. We didn't know what they would want from us. So when we turned onto this Makadem road, we realised what would happen to us, because it was dark, 12, 10.00 in the evening. There were no facilities, not a kilometre around, and you immediately know what will happen to you. We were panic-stricken. We started panicking. We started asking, "Where are you taking us," and questions like this. So this route, this Makadem route, leads to a garbage dump heap where you threw garbage into -- it was a kind of cliff through which you throw the garbage. We stopped some 100 metres close to that cliff, and from that, we were ordered to leave the car and to walk towards this garbage dump. So we started panicking simply, because when you have to walk into the darkness, you know what will happen. And my twin brother asked one of these soldiers, "Why are you doing this to us? I went to school yesterday and you want to kill me now. Why are you doing this?" And he was very rude, and he said, "This is for the Central Bosnia," because at that time in the Croatian media, Central Bosnia was mentioned and spoken about all the time, because their media would mention at that time that Croats were butchered and killed in Central Bosnia, which was not true at all. And when we were then close to this garbage dump, they ordered us to sit down, to kneel down, what is a typical position for being shot at, for being executed. And when we did this, one of them, all three of them, actually, went away from us, two metres, one metre, and they discussed something. This discussion lasted for about five seconds. And after that, one of them comes forward and prepares his gun. That was an automatic gun, rifle, and shoots at the four of us. And it was a burst and the intention to kill us. My older brother and my mother, when they saw that he is preparing the rifle, repeating the rifle, they got up and walked towards them, and all these bullets, they actually collected all the bullets with their bodies, so that's how they saved our lives. And the remains of the bullets by which we were hit, the remaining bullets, we both fell down off this cliff where you throw the garbage into, and my brother -- my older brother and my mother remained on the top of the ravine because they walked towards them so they couldn't fall down.
