I don't know. I can't explain that. I was unconscious maybe for five seconds, but the moment when I was conscious again, I was calling my brother, my twin brother. He did the same. I don't know, actually, why I did this, I just knew that he was alive. I had that feeling that he is alive, that my twin brother is alive. So we called each other and we started climbing up. It was about ten metres, the ravine was about 10 metres high. And when we finally arrived up there, during that time, while we were unconscious and while we were climbing, these soldiers who committed that crime left that place thinking that we were dead as well. As we fell down, no one doubted that -- they thought that we were dead as well. So the two of us climbed up. I must say, we almost walked over the corpses of my older brother and my mother. We didn't really look at them because if I had seen that, I would not be now in front of this court, because a normal person cannot survive this. The closest family member full of blood, you can't. So we continued walking towards the main road, and after ten metres, my brother fell as he was hit by five bullets into his legs. After the first few seconds, he could walk because the wounds were still warm, so he couldn't feel the pain, so he could walk. So it was only after a minute that he fell down and he couldn't continue walking. As I was only lightly wounded in the area where my kidneys are, only by one bullet, I could continue walking. I started looking for help, and as the closest road where there was heavy traffic was the road to Citluk, I started walking towards that road, and I stopped one car. It was a carriage or it was a type of truck with no license plates, and I was all in blood as my trousers were bloody. I showed this man that I was wounded, that my brother is lying down there. I thought at that time that my brother was dead because I didn't know what the wounds were like. I told him that my brother was lying down there. I asked him for help and to call for help. And he answered very rudely, "Are you still alive?" And offensive language, you Muslim bastard, something similar to that. I saw that there was no further reason to stop a car, because if I would expose myself to some further danger, if they did not finish up, maybe someone else would finish what these soldiers left. I started walking towards the top of the hill because that was somewhere in the middle of the hill, so I started walking towards the top, because I couldn't really orientate myself where Mostar was. And from there I saw into which direction it is, and then I started walking towards Mostar. When I was going down, I could hear how my brother was calling for help. And if a car would pass this main road, then my brother, as he was lying on the earth, he would call, "Help me, help me, I'm here." And I could hear those calls, and I knew when a car was arriving in that way. So that I could hide. I could not be seen from the road. So I was going down like this for about an hour until I arrived to some suburbs of Mostar, and I saw lights in front of the house. People were probably celebrating something. You could see that they were drinking and eating while I was dying there. They were celebrating and I went down and I told them who I was and what happened. I had to explain that I was not a member of the BH army, that I'm coming from the city. I don't know what I was really talking. I was just saying things. They called or they sent one boy to one checkpoint where there was the village police. This was not the normal police. These were only people who organised themselves, they organised their own police, their guards. So they sent this boy, and afterwards, two men arrived after about ten minutes. They took me and said, "Let's go down to the checkpoint," to the place where they were. And when we got down, at that time, they called the ambulance. These people helped. They did as much as they could. So they called the ambulance, and after ten, fifteen minutes, the ambulance arrives. The driver who was driving this ambulance asked me, "Do you want me to take you to the new hospital or to the old hospital?" And I said, as he was -- as there was an acquaintance of the family, a doctor lady who worked in the old hospital, she worked in that old hospital, I decided for the old hospital. I forgot to mention something beforehand, that in the period during the 9th of May and the 30th of June, when most of the Muslim population was released from the camps, when they were collecting people on the 9th of May, there is a new tactic introduced by the HVO. People were gathering from buildings and they were divided into groups, men, old people, women, and children, and all the others who could not fight, the population who could not fight. That population was taken to the left side of the river and to quicken this process of the blockade, as many hungry mouths as possible that was good for them. And those who were capable to fight, they were taken back again to the Heliodrom against the protest of the international community. And while we were going from the right side to the left side, there was some shooting, there was shooting at people who were going from the right side to the left side. And a lot of people died in that way. That's how there was fear in Mostar. If they take you, you will probably end up between the right and the left bank when you are crossing the line. So, we, as a family, when our turn came, when our building had to be taken to the left bank, we were hiding in a doctor's apartment, I guess, her place, and she was working at the old hospital, and she had some connections to the HVO, and her apartment was under the protection of the HVO. We were hiding there for five days and after that, the situation in Mostar improved, and we were able to return to our apartment again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Dragan, the events you've just talked about, about going to the left bank and the assistance of this doctor, that took place during the 9 May, 30 June time frame; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to correct you. We did not go to the left bank of the Neretva river, to the place of that doctor, it was on the right bank. But that house was protected by the Croatian Defence Council. That's was the reason why the HVO troops never entered that building, but it did happen in that period, between the 9th of May and the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the connection to your story is that this doctor worked at the old hospital and that's one of the reasons why you chose to go to the old hospital after you were shot on the 30th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's only logical that you should go to see those people who have already helped you. When I arrived in the old hospital, I was admitted by the medical personnel there, and I received medical treatment for my wounds. After that, members of the security in that hospital, these were mostly people from Mostar, who did not want to fire at their own people, at the people that they knew from the right bank, these were Croats who refused to shoot at their erstwhile friends with whom they had lived their whole lives. At any rate, these soldiers who provided security in the hospital were people from Mostar. I recognised one of them. He was a friend of my older brother's, and after I explained to him what had happened and that my brother is still lying there at the scene where this whole thing had happened. I did not have any hopes that my brother would survive at all. I just explained to him where this location was, the place where my brother was lying. Since I was not familiar with the environment of the city, I was only able to describe to him what this place looked like, and he drew the conclusion as to where that place actually was. He then went with two of his friends, who also were in the security of the hospital, in an ambulance to search for my brother. After a few hours, he was also brought to the hospital. Actually, it wasn't hours. He was brought within half an hour to the old hospital. This is the same place where I was. When I saw him, it is only then that I lost consciousness. Somehow, things were easier for me, and I simply let go. I was drained of all strength. My brother, he was seriously injured, and he was placed in the intensive care, the place where the most seriously wounded people were put, and I was in a normal room. And all this time, my father was in the camp, and he was not aware of what had happened to us, to the rest of his family. Since they realised again that they had picked up the sick people from those buildings and they brought the sick people to the camp, when I say "they," I mean the Croatian troops, they set up a medical commission, and this medical commission would release people on the basis of their diagnosis. They let them go back home or they would even refer them to a hospital. Since this commission released my father, he had had the kidney surgery, he had renal stones and he had been urinating blood. That was the reason why he was allowed to go to the hospital, and he was released from the camp. Naturally, he went straight home to see where his closest relatives were. When he came home he saw, in front of the entrance to the building, many women whose husbands or sons had been taken away on that day by the Croatian troops. And since, of course, those mothers wanted to know where their husbands were, whether they were alive and well, they asked my father, and he actually wanted to avoid that, because any large gathering of the Muslim population would be dangerous, not only for him, but also for the others, women, and all those people who wanted to get that information. He decided to send a lady neighbour from the next door building because he had entered the building next door. He did not go straight to our house, to check whether our door, the door to our apartment was locked, because if it had been locked, it would mean that we had gone to the place of that lady doctor who hid us in that period up until the 30th. Or if the door had been broken down, then that would mean that we had been picked up. The neighbour checked this and she told him that the door was locked and that nobody answered the door, but it was just locked. My father hoped that we were safe. He thought that we had gone into hiding in the doctor's place. And since she worked in the old hospital, he went to visit her at her work place. And when he came there, he learned from her what had happened, what had happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, prior to that time, did your father know that your oldest brother and his wife, your mother, had been murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He learned of my brother's and my mother's deaths from that lady doctor, since she worked at that place where we were admitted. That was five days after the crime had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during the five-day period of time after the crime and when your father came to the hospital, were you and your brother visited by any HV troops that came looking for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what the doctors knew in that five-day period, and since my brother saw one of the soldiers, he, again, recognised the soldiers who had arrived on the 30th of June to take us to be executed. They came there to finish what they had started. Through the intervention of the Mostar doctors, they were prevented from doing that, and since, I assume, there were many witnesses, they postponed doing that for some other day. In that five-day period, while my father was away, they came on one occasion to take us away, to finish their task. When my father learned from the doctor what had happened, and since he already had the referral slip for that hospital, he was given that by the medical commission, he was admitted to the hospital and he remained there with us in the same room. Twenty days later, a member of the Croatian forces came to that room, the hospital room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, again, Croatian or HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who came to your room and what force did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same persons who came to commit that crime on the 30th of June. Those were the members of the military police of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The HV? Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty days after that event, one of them came again. This time, it wasn't a person that we knew. It was a member of the Croatian forces dressed in a black uniform. As soon as he came to the door of the room, he immediately approached my father, pointed at him with his index finger, and said to the nurse who happened to be in the room at the time, "If this guy disappears," meaning my father, "you will be responsible." And then he left the room, probably in order to talk to the doctor again. We learned later just from some people that on that day, because a doctor asked my father whether he wanted to go to the funeral that was taking place on that very same day or not -- first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The funeral for whom, Dragan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The funeral for my older brother and my mother, the funeral rites since they were in the morgue of the new hospital. He asked my father whether he wanted to attend the funeral, and since my father knew that this would be no funeral in accordance with the Muslim rights, since he knew that the Muslim priest, the Hodza, wouldn't be there, and since he didn't want to leave us again, he had left us once before, and the misfortune befell us. This was the reason why he did not want to go. And it turned out later that these men had been waiting for my father and for us at the funeral, because if we had left the hospital, it would have been easy for them to pick us up. When they saw that we would not be attending the funeral, they went to the hospital in an attempt to take us away again. The Mostar doctors intervened once again. They had already called the police. The police arrived in a few minutes. The police confronted those people who wanted to take us away. At that time, the police was not carrying out its duties. Any normal police would, of course, arrest those people. They did not know what to do. In fact, because the police in that area turned a blind eye on anything. They approved of everything. If somebody killed a Muslim, the police never intervened. At any rate, these police officers, for reasons unknown to us, removed those persons from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these were HVO police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normal police -- normal members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they removed HV soldiers from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. There has been a misunderstanding. The people who came to pick us up, to take us away, these were members of the HVO, HVO. Other people, not those people who committed the crime. And they were removed from the hospital by the normal police of the Herceg-Bosna. So this incident passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, did you get a visit at any point during this time from any member of the intelligence service of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot to mention the fact that between the first and the second arrival of those people, of those forces, the soldiers that wanted to take us away, a member of the SIS, Security Information Service, came. First he asked the two of us to accompany him to the hospital corridor. When we left, he told us that he was a colonel in the SIS, and he showed his ID card. I can't now recall his name. He asked us whether we knew anything about a crime that had happened. I assume, since the crime was probably or definitely committed by the Croatian army, they sent in their intelligence officer to see whether we were dangerous for them at all, whether we knew that these people were Croatian army or not, because at that time, in the media, there were reports about the Croatian army soldiers having been noticed, seen in Bosnia. He wanted to check whether we knew that these were Croatian army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say "Croatian army soldiers," you mean HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, members of the HV. After that, since I realised that it would serve no purpose for me to say that these were Croatian army soldiers, that I would be bringing myself into an unnecessary risk if I were to admit that these were Croatian army soldiers, that way I would pose a risk for them. That's why I said that these were uncontrolled groups of soldiers who committed that crime. I said that I did not know who they were precisely, but that this was simply some soldiers who were acting independently, and they were not under anyone's orders. He then was under the impression that I did not know anything and the actual situation was on the contrary. I knew everything. He was happy with the answer. He said, "All right, guys, if we learn anything about who had done that, we will let you know," and he left. And that's how this case was closed, in fact. Then 20 days later after the second arrival of those men, when they wanted to take us to finish us off, there was a mass arrival of wounded Muslims in the hospital where we were. Those wounded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Kehoe, perhaps we could take a break. These are very painful events that are being told by this young man. Perhaps we can stop now and then start up again at 4.30, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume the hearing. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Becirovic, are you all right? Do you feel okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Did you rest up a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We can resume. Mr. Kehoe, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, you were just about to talk to the period of time when there was a large influx of wounded coming into that hospital. Before we talk about that, let me just ask a few clarifying questions that have been noted by my colleagues. The first question that I would like to ask you is: You mentioned after you were arrested, your older brother, your mother and your twin Goran were arrested, by the HV soldiers, you passed through various checkpoints, and you noted that the people at the checkpoint must have been familiar with these HV soldiers because they waved them through quite easily; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these soldiers at the checkpoints HVO soldiers or HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were HVO soldiers, together with members of the police of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next point of clarification has to deal with the HV soldiers driving to a military headquarters at University of Mostar. Was that the HVO headquarters or HV headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the headquarters of the HVO military police, not HVO, but military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The last point of clarification, and this is a minor clarification, has to deal with the distance between the van at the location at the garbage dump and where you were shot. I believe the transcript had noted it was 100 metres away. Was it less than 100 metres or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said "100 metres," I meant 10 metres. I actually mean 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go back to your story. Sir, did there come a time when there was a large influx of wounded when you were transferred to another section of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, while we were in the old room where we arrived on the 30th of June, a lot of wounded people were brought to the hospital. Some of them were even lying in the corridors because the hospital didn't have enough beds for all of them. Later on, the doctors suggested, because it was safer for us and because they would get some free beds, we were taken to another part of the hospital which was not used. Because it could be shelled, because of that, we were transferred to this part of the hospital. In the meantime, that Friday we called Black Friday, because around 30 to 35, maybe even more, patients were taken care of even in the corridors. We didn't have enough doctors. The nurses helped to heal the wounds. At that time, these people arrived to the hospital, they were taken care of, and all of those who were only slightly wounded by maybe some shrapnel, they could be released. The heavily wounded, the seriously injured people stayed at the hospital. We were very close to that place. We could talk to these prisoners. These prisoners were explaining that they were digging -- not digging. They were making a kind of shelter for the Croatian soldiers in this Santic Street. In this Santic Street, the street fights were very heavy. They were fighting one house after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, let me clarify certain things. The prisoners that were brought in that were wounded, were they Bosnian Muslim prisoners that were doing this work when they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were Bosniak Muslims, only Bosniak Muslims. Later on, these prisoners --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hold on. One more question, Dragan, by way of clarification. You noted in the transcript that they were making a kind of shelter for the Croatian soldiers. Were these HVO soldiers that they were making the shelter for when they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As at the beginning, the BH army would allow that the prisoners would make a kind of shelter for the Croatian army so that they could take some buildings without any losses. But when they realised that the Croatian soldiers could come forward very quickly in that way, they started to wound these prisoners. They wanted just to wound them, to injure them. They shot at their hands or their legs so that there were no serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Dragan, the word that's coming off in the transcript is "Croatian soldiers." Were these HVO soldiers that were using the prisoners to dig these shelters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were HVO soldiers. As the lines in Mostar, in the city, were kept by -- the positions were held by HVO. And members of the Croatian army, they used them when they needed help. That's what I found out from one patient whose cousin came to visit, and that cousin of that patient who was lying together with us was a policeman, a policeman of the Herceg-Bosna Police. He was bragging about the Tigers that were special units of the Croatian army who were coming from Zagreb, that they have taken one hill in ten minutes that the army had taken already before. That's how I found out that members of the Croatian army, not that they were only in Mostar, but that they also took part in the fights for Mostar, around Mostar. From that, you can see that these soldiers were used for some special actions. When they realised that the soldiers of the HVO army were not capable enough to do something alone, to take something or to defend something, then special units of the Croatian army, I think they are HV, special units mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was one of these special units that assisted the HVO the Tigers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Tigers from Zagreb. They didn't fight only in Mostar. They fought all over in Bosnia where it was necessary, where the BH and the HVO were fighting. So to come back to my story with the prisoners, HVO soldiers were using prisoners in that way, that they would be a kind of shelter, and then they would come forward and take building by building. These same prisoners --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. In the translation, are you saying that they used these prisoners as a shelter or used them as a shield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were using them predominantly to make shelters. But when the BH army would attack some buildings that the HVO army would control, then they would use them as shelter, as a shield so that they could not take that building. I can give an example. The hotel called Ero where older people used to live, it was a nursing home, it was attacked by the BH army. And by using these people as human shields, they prevented this hotel from being taken. That's one of the examples how they would use people as human shields. Otherwise, they would use these people to make shelters or a kind of protection or fortification out of which then these soldiers would shoot at the BH army. At that time, a lot of people lost their lives, they weren't only injured as the Croatians. I think by that, the soldiers of the HVO army, these people were dying, and that they were from Mostar. And people knew each other, and they knew that they would have to continue living with these people afterwards. They started using people from other places, like, for example, from Blagaj, from Bosna. I could find out about that from people who would arrive to the hospital and who were from Blagaj. When I said "Blagaj," I meant Maglaj. Blagaj is a completely different place than Maglaj. I meant Maglaj. Maglaj is in the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These prisoners were captured by Serbian soldiers who were fighting at the Maglaj front. Later on, these prisoners, I don't know why, these prisoners were given to the HVO soldiers, and then they would transfer these people to the camps, to Heliodrom and other camps, in the west of Herzegovina. These people, as they were not registered at the International Red Cross, there was actually no trace in international organisations, these people were used as human shields. And it was mostly them that would get killed. This was continued. This lasted all the time. The hospital was only 200 metres away from the first front-line, 200 to 300 metres, where these human shields were being used. I mean by that, the Santic Street. These wounded people would be taken immediately to the hospital. So chaos occurred in these hospitals in the western side of Mostar. Later on, to calm down the situation, they didn't attack anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple questions, Dragan, about this issue. Were the people that were being used as human shields Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these were Bosnian Muslims. Later on, those people from Maglaj that were used, they were also Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the HVO use any methods to make sure that these Muslims did not run away when they were working on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was always a danger that the prisoner could escape to the side of the BH army as he is going as the first one. And then ten metres behind him, there is a Croatian soldier, and it is easy for him to run away to the Bosnian side, I mean, to the BH army side. That's why the Croatian soldiers invented the following: That they had a chain, and people were chained around their necks, and they were then led to make those shelters. They couldn't run away as they were tied with these chains. That's some examples that happened. For example, one of the prisoners ran away in that way because he took off this chain that he had around his neck. I don't know how he did it. He tied that chain around a certain tree and that's how he ran away. The Croatian soldier thought that he was on his chain, as he was pulling, and he could see that he could tighten up the chain, and that's how people ran away. The other way was people, they would use a father and a son as a kind of guarantee that somebody would not run away. For example, you keep the son on the Croatian side and you send the father to make those shelters or fortifications. And then if the father would run away, they would kill the son. So no per cent of people -- zero per cent of people would run away. These are all examples of how they tried to secure that people don't run onto the Bosnian side, I mean by that, the BH army side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned that some Bosnian Muslims from Maglaj were also wounded while they were digging on the frontlines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. During the first period, when they started using these human shields, it was mostly people from Mostar. Later on, as I said, they used people from Maglaj and they spared the people from Mostar. These people from Blagaj, they came to the hospital and they would tell us these stories, and that's how I know what happened on the front-line, how people managed, how they ran away, how they -- for example, a Croatian soldier, he would throw away a piece of bread, he would throw it among them, and then they would fight for this piece of bread. All these stories how a human being was tortured. These prisoners had no rights anymore. They were not registered at the International Red Cross. There were no signs of their lives. Everybody could do with them what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, did you receive any information from any of these Bosnian Muslim wounded from Maglaj that they were digging trenches for the HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As these prisoners were arriving, they came, they were dirty, and they had blood on their clothes. As we were healthy, we would help them to change their clothes, to put on clean clothes, underwear. And from their stories, from what they saw, they told us what was happening. All that information that I have about the human shields comes from these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did they ever inform you that they were digging trenches for the HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not only did they tell me that, but they were also explaining how they were digging and how they were used by the HVO to be used as a human shield or to make shelters for the Croatian soldiers so that they could shoot later on onto the soldiers of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, before we end before your departure, let me ask you: During this time period when you were in this other wing of the hospital, did the HVO military police come to you concerning an investigation of the murder of your older brother and your mother and, if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact day when that happened, but it was in the morning. Two policemen entered into our room, HVO military police, and they had a kind of order that we should go with them to make a testimony so that we could witness for a certain reason. We don't know why. Later on, we decided with our father -- later on, we found out what they wanted, but we agreed with our father if there would be a certain trial, that we had to go there, because one person was accused, among other things, for the murder of two HVO soldiers on the front-line. That person was also a member of the HVO. They wanted to find this person guilty for our crime so that they could indict him for our crime, and it wasn't him who did that. That's why we had to go with them to the military court. That was at the headquarters of the military police at the university. Among those buildings, there was also the military court. Before we left, we agreed with our father that if we would recognise this person, that he was the one who committed the crime, we would say that it was not him. Because if we would become witnesses again in a certain situation where the war was still going on, nobody could guarantee our safety for our testifying in front of a court. Because of that, we decided, even if we would recognise this person, we would say that it was not that person and that we don't know him. That's what we agreed with our father beforehand. When we arrived at the court, we were introduced to a certain person that we saw for the first time in our life. According to them, we had to testify, each individually. That means one had to stay outside in front of the door of the court and the other one had to say if it was him or not virtually (sic). I talked to the soldiers, and I heard from them when my brother testified while I was waiting outside -- from the soldiers who guarded me, I learned that that soldier had killed Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Two HVO soldiers or HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers. To the north of Mostar, at the front-line there, there had been a quarrel, and two HVO soldiers were killed by that person. They said that he had committed several other murders, murders of Muslims and Serbs. There was also a Serb waiting there. He was also supposed to testify whether that was the person who committed the crime against a Serbian family. At any rate, that person was not tried for the Muslims or Serbs that he had killed. He was being tried exclusively for having killed two Croatian soldiers. Since there was an international pressure on the Croatian side to solve those crimes, they wanted to pin all those crimes to a single person in order to show to the international community certain results, as if some of the crimes that had been committed were solved and that people were punished for those crimes. That person that was presented to us was not the perpetrator of the crime against my family. There were three people who participated in that crime anyway, not just one. The name of that person who was accused of the killing, I don't know his name, but my father knows his name. When we said that we did not recognise that person as the killer of our brother and mother, they let us go and we returned to the hospital. This trial was a farce. It was a travesty. It was held just to show to the international community that something was done about those crimes. They simply wanted to pin all the crimes onto one person. That person had already killed two Croatian soldiers, and they wanted to solve all of this very quickly. They wanted to sentence him either to life imprisonment or even to death penalty, and they simply wanted to pin all the crimes on him. When we testified and we said that this was not the person, as, indeed, he wasn't, we were returned to the hospital. In the meantime, my father waited for four hours for us to return. He went through all those things that a parent can go through, all the worries. "Where are my children? Why did I let them go?" All those concerns of a parent, he had to go through all that. He did not accompany us, because he thought if we were to be taken away to be killed, if all of us were to be killed, then there wouldn't be any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, let me just take you back. When you got back to the hospital, you stayed in the hospital until about the 27th of September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27th of September, approximately. I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you another question, Dragan. Shortly before that, did the HVO make a decision that the patients in the hospital would be removed back to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The patients from the hospital, not only were there the wounded, the ones that had been used as human shields, but you also had normal patients, people who had usual illnesses, such as the renal stones. All the prisoners who were brought in to be treated in the hospital, they were picked up by the Croatian Defence Council as soon as they got well. They had no protection from the doctors. They did not have any special treatment. They were treated as prisoners. You mentioned sick people being picked up. That was the reason why we left the hospital. Because the hospital, for us, was like the house of Anna Frank, that's where we hid from the Croatian soldiers, because as soon as we left the hospital, we would be taken away and caught by those people who committed those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, Dragan, let me ask you: Based on the fact that the patients were being sent back out to the Heliodrom, did you, with your father and your twin brother, make a decision that it was time to leave Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That taking away of prisoners, it was not something that was done en masse. That was the cleansing. That's what I call it. The hospital was cleansed of all the Muslim patients, and that's what happened two days before we were to leave for a third country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, so that the Judges can follow you more easily, when you're asked a question, try to answer it precisely. There's a precise question. Try to answer precisely. I know it's difficult. These were very, very hard experiences for you, but so that the Judges can understand you and follow you, and the Defence as well -- you are telling a story. You're asked a question. Please answer the question as precisely as possible, all right? Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, would you ask your question again, please, the one having to do with the prisoners, the way that they left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, after you observed these prisoners being sent back to the Heliodrom from the hospital, you and your father and your brother made a decision to leave Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I would just like to say something. Those prisoners were taken away to the Heliodrom immediately, and the cleansing of the hospital took place during just one day. The whole hospital was cleansed of all the Muslim patients. And the taking away of prisoners to the Heliodrom, that happened every day. This was the first time, however, that all the patients were taken to the Heliodrom, I mean, the Muslim patients. Even though they were on stretchers, even though they had I.V. lines in or they had some serious medical conditions -- I even know a person who was taken away even though he had had surgery just one day before that, and he had an open wound. Those people who were taken away were Muslim patients who were in the hospital. With the exception of the three of us, we were able to remain there, myself, my brother and my father, and another lad whose relatives worked in the hospital. That's how he stayed in the hospital. The reason why we stayed in the hospital was because the doctors had intervened on our behalf. They did not let them take us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, so ultimately, on the 27th of September, you left Mostar, went to Zagreb with the assistance of the UNHCR, and then you and your father and your brother emigrated to a third country; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dragan, thank you very much. I have no further questions. Thank you Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Turning to the Defence, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Well, actually, good evening. You testimony was rather long, and now I will ask you a general question. What you told us this afternoon, is this what you know, what you knew at the time when this was happening in 1993 when you were a student aged 14, or did you combine that knowledge with the information you received later? So are you speaking purely from what you knew at the time or did you add something that you learned later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all the things that I know and which I presented here, this is my personal experience. I have no knowledge from a third person, that is, the knowledge of some other events where I was not present. I learned about that directly from those persons who were present while those events were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, the first matter that I have to ask you about: You say that civilians were released under the pressure of the international community, that 7.000 civilians were released. You are a 14-year-old boy. You are hiding like Anna Frank in apartments. How do you know that the Croatian authorities in Mostar made the decision because of the pressure of the international community, and how do you know that 7.000 civilians were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 7.000 people, that's only in comparison to the 8.000 people. I don't know the exact number, but out of the 8.000, 7.000 were released. So that's the ratio. That's what I stated. So how many people were actually released?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But my question was different. How do you know how many people were released and how do you know that the HVO authorities released those people under the pressure of the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was because it was on TV. The Spanish TV filmed people being taken away to the stadium, and then from the stadium to the Heliodrom on the 9th of May. That's why the international community exerted pressure, to have these things stopped so that these people can go back to their homes. The reason why they were taken away is because they were Muslims and not because they posed any risk to the Croatian side. The only reason was the fact that they were Muslim. Let me answer your question about the 7.000 and 8.000. As I said, I can't give you an exact number of how many prisoners there were. Not even Croats know that. They just picked up everyone, all those people they didn't like. You can't keep records of that, because all the people -- some of the people who were sick were released immediately the same day or after five days, after ten days. So I just gave you some kind of a ratio, the proportion. Out of 8.000, 7.000 were released and another thousand remained in prison. These were mostly people who posed some kind of risk to the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the decision of the Croatian authorities is something that you reconstructed in accordance with the things broadcast on TV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was my conclusion. It's only logical that if you see something on TV, if you see that people are being taken away to an unknown fate into the camps, the international community, of course, feels that if has to intervene against such actions undertaken by the Croatian side. It's only natural that there was enormous pressure, because only Hitler did things like that in 1941. You know that, of course, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, when you answer, please turn to the Judges. Listen to Mr. Nobilo's questions, but then you answer facing the Judges, all right? I didn't get the answer to that. I didn't have an interpretation for the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was waiting for the interpretation. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was asking you to be sure that when you answer Mr. Nobilo's questions, you turn to the Judges, that you are answering directly to the Judges, all right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This pressure by the international community had to be exerted because it was already official. It had already been broadcast on TV. The Spanish teams, the Spanish journalists, they recorded all that. It was in all the media in Europe, even in the United States. And that was the reason why these governments exerted pressure to have these people released. What would be the reason, otherwise, for the Croatian authorities to release those people they had picked up and taken to the camps? Because there is no reason why you should arrest somebody and release him the next day. They wanted to have those people detained over a prolonged period of time because it would be easier for them to control these people, and that's why the camps were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said it was in all the media in Europe and the United States. You saw that as a 14-year-old boy in Mostar caught up in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, among other things, it was on HTV. Maybe you don't know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, I would like to interrupt. I feel there's some difficulty here and I would like to clear it up. You've been called by the Prosecutor to testify about what you experienced, and it was very painful to you. What are you studying now? You say you're a student. What are you studying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm getting ready to study at the Faculty of Economics. Then when I get my diploma, I will be able to enrol in the Faculty of Economics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I certainly hope that you are successful. You're helping the Judges through your testimony. You must understand that it's necessary, and I know it's hard, you have to try to separate what you experienced yourself, and Lord knows that you experienced very, very difficult things, but as much as possible, try to isolate all of the knowledge that you have or all the judgements that you've made, all your opinions, you have a right to your opinion, of course, and they are respectable opinions, but try, please -- you cannot testify in front of any court, whether it be here today or in another place tomorrow in your own country, you cannot testify about something that you haven't experienced yourself or perceived yourself. If occasionally you give an opinion, that's normal, but you have to remain, as much as possible, within the framework of what you yourself experienced. You are a witness to something. Would you try to do that, please? Very well. We're going to continue the cross-examination, but try to make the distinction between what you yourself experienced and what you want to say about the conflict. I'm sure you have many things you would like to say, but for the time being, you are a witness to certain events, and it's about those events that the Prosecutor has asked you to testify. I've spent a little time on this, but it's for your own interests and in the interests of justice. All right, Mr. Nobilo, will you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you said to the Prosecutor that you were going to school and that you had to hide the fact that you were a Muslim, that you had to speak Croatian in order to hide that fact. Did you go to the same school with the same teachers and the same colleagues or did you change the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I continued to go to the same school, that's the Fifth Primary School on the other bank, but normally -- I can't really recall which primary school it was, but that school was shut down because it was close to the frontlines, and that's why I went to the Fifth Primary. Otherwise, in that school that I went to before, we did not have Croatian language as a subject. And now I had to go to that school where I had Croatian as the subject, and I had to speak Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question was whether you had the same students (sic) as your colleagues and the same teachers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you then manage to hide the fact that you were a Muslim, since both the teachers and the pupils knew you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hide that from the teachers, since the teachers knew us, but I hid that from other pupils. When they moved to the school, I met a lot of new pupils. I had to hide the fact that I was a Muslim from them in order to avoid any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said to the Prosecutor, furthermore, that anyone could kill a Muslim without being held responsible for that. How do you know that? Can you give us an example of a person being killed that you witnessed yourself, that you knew who the perpetrator was and that he was not held responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any killing, because if I had, it's possible that I maybe wouldn't be here. At any rate, I did not witness any killings. But I knew about that theory, that any Croat could kill a Muslim without being prosecuted for it on the basis of an example that happened in the period between the 9th of May and the 30th of June when Muslims were found at garbage dumps. And although the murderer was known, he went away scot free, not because the police were unable to arrest him, but because they did not want to arrest him, although they knew his address. I forgot now the name of the killer and the name of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you don't know the name of the victim or of the killer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot. I don't know. I just forgot, because there are so many incidents in that period, and I simply forgot about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that your brother was employed in the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, and that your mother used to work for the MUP before the war. Can you explain to the Judges what is MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: MUP is the Ministry of the Interior. That's the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did your father do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked on road construction, Nisko Gradna (phoen). That's the construction company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, when talking about the events on the 30th of June, you said that people in Eastern Mostar were hungry. How do you know that they were starving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, why would people be throwing packages of food from planes into Eastern Mostar if they were not starving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why would they starve then if they had those packages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because that was not enough for all those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know how many packages were delivered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the planes -- when those packages were thrown from the planes, I saw that personally. It was not enough to supply all the population there. I'd think that you would need several thousand planes to supply 50,000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know, was that the only source of supplies, whether they were UNHCR convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Convoys were let go if the HVO decided to do so. They were at the mercy of the HVO. When they saw that they did not have enough food to survive, and when the international community exerted a lot of pressure to release those convoys, then they had to do it, not because they wanted to, but they had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know that they didn't want to do that out of their desire to help people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostar was blocked. Why didn't they allow people to leave Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You described that a battalion of HVO containing mostly Muslims went over to the area controlled by the BH army and that they managed to liberate Bijelo Polje in this manner. Can you please tell me, how do you know that? Is this something you learned in Mostar during the time that you were in hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this information because one Muslim who was a member of the HVO was there during the attack. He was at the northern camp at that time, and that was the target of the attack of the BH army, and he managed to get back to the right bank. And from his story, I know he came the same day, the 30th of June. From his story, I know that a lot of soldiers of Bosnian nationality, I mean by that Muslim soldiers, HV soldiers, that they became members of the Bosnian army. That's how I know. So that's how this surrounding was broken within two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So when this surrounding was broken, do you know if there was any communication with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know, is it familiar to you, that there was mobilisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was that because there was war going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know how old the men had to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 18 further on to a certain age. I don't know how old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that on the night of the 30th of June until midnight, about 8.000 Muslims were collected. How do you know that? How do you know that that action was over at midnight? How do you know that it was 8.000 people and not 7.000 or 6.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the same number that was on the 9th of May, and I know that this action of gathering people lasted, because along that road to Citluk, there were buses passing by, buses who were taking those prisoners. They were transporting them. As I was walking down after the crime into the city, I saw those buses, how they were still passing by. That's how I could conclude that this was going on until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that these soldiers, these HV military policemen, who took you, your twin brother, your mother and your older brother, you said that these were HV insignia. What kind of insignia were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These insignia, they were white, and it says "HV military police." They had badges on which -- it's something similar to the police badges with which you can present yourself and say that you are HV military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You also said that these HV military policemen were from Dalmatia and that you can recognise their accents. Can you recognise out of which region I am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot recognise you personally. I can only guess. I know the Stikalan (phoen) dialect, I can't say, but in Mostar, there were a lot of people who would come from Split, and that's how I knew because very good friends. A brother from one of the neighbours was personally coming from Split, so that's why I could recognise that accent. According to your question about your accent, I can't answer that. I was born in Split. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Further on, you said that their propaganda, HVO propaganda, was saying that in Central Bosnia the Croats are being killed and that that was not true at all, that that was far away from the truth. Can you tell us, what do you know about the Central Bosnia, because we are trying to figure out for a year now what was going on in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what I know from the media, because I was not in Central Bosnia, but I guess -- I don't guess, I know that these crimes, so many crimes, could not be committed with regard to how many crimes were committed against the Muslim population. Because if these crimes had been so serious, then there would be no Muslims in Herzegovina. That's how harsh the reaction would be in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That truck that stopped after they killed your family, and that driver cursed you or was rude towards you, was that driver a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a soldier, because the civilians could not move at that time. It was curfew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Further on, you said that normal police, Herceg-Bosna police, protected you in a way at the hospital. Can you tell me, what do you mean by "normal police"? Do you mean civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean, civilian police. They had to protect us because they had arrived there. They couldn't allow that in front of them somebody could be taken and killed within an hour. I know of no police in the world that would allow such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This colonel that came to visit you, did he show any kind of identification to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He identified himself with some kind of a document. I can't remember now. But since we were just boys, we did not look at the document, at the ID. But I did know that this was a SIS ID. I recognised it as a SIS ID. It's not that I knew that from before. I just recognised it there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was he nice to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He tried to determine, to learn from you, who it was that did that crime, whether they were members of the Croatian army -- please allow me to finish the question and then you will give me your answer. Why did you conclude or why didn't you conclude that he is really trying to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know why a colonel of SIS would come to us, to the hospital, because there were also other organisations who could do that, who could find out the facts, not a SIS colonel who has got completely given tasks. Was that a danger to the Croatian nation? I apologise for my expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Don't you know what SIS is? That's the Security and Information Service, and the main task of the SIS is to protect the security of the army. So that's why they conduct investigations of crimes committed by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the security of the soldiers, how their lives were endangered. These were civilians, crimes committed against civilians, and that's why I thought it was up to them to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that's why you decided it was not an investigation but something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would just ask that counsel allow the witness to finish his answer before he interrupts with another question, which has happened. The question he was given was cut off at the end, and, as you can see from the transcript, "... that's why I thought it was up to them to ..." then an ellipses when counsel breaks in with another question. I simply ask that counsel allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, please allow the answer to be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Without mentioning any names, can you tell me whether in your neighbourhood, in your street, were there any other cases of such executions as there was in your family? Any of your neighbours, were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my personal knowledge, I know from a school colleague of mine that his parents were -- actually, his grandparents, that they were in the same way, even in a worse way, killed. There are many examples that I can't remember today, but I remember that example because that boy went to the same school with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I don't know if it's appropriate, but I would like to get some names for identification purposes so that we can conduct an investigation. We did not have the statement of this witness in advance. So that we can present evidence during our case. So if you feel that this would endanger anyone, we can now go into closed session. I would like to just learn some names of the family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have any objections to that. Of course, we will have to vacate that area there, or if you go into private session, I suppose there's no need to vacate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Actually, it would be sufficient to switch off the tone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Private session. We can do that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In this courtroom, that isn't possible. We can't have private sessions in this courtroom. It has to be closed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then it's closed. We're back to square one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, at the end of my cross-examination, we can ask all those questions, so we can go into closed session at the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That would be the best solution. About how much time do you still need, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Not too much, fifteen minutes, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. That would be the best solution then. Then we'll have a closed session for the last questions in your cross-examination, and then we will go back to public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told us about human shields in the Santic Street in the defence of the Ero Hotel. Can you please tell us, how do you know about that, who told you about that, and which people were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That information I got from prisoners who would get wounded while they were used as human shields, for example, a human shield for the protection of the Hotel Ero. I don't know their names because I didn't write down in my diary, write down their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know that the people who were arrested in Maglaj, that they were not registered with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because that's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who told you about the use of the chains as the security device to prevent the prisoners from escaping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also what the prisoners told me, because I was taking care of these prisoners. They needed help to clean themselves. They were dirty. We would give them our own clothes so that they could change. That's how we started talking with them, and that's how I found out about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person who told you that and who was tied up with the chain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who told me this didn't tell me his name. And even if he had told me his name, I would not remember it; I couldn't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The case when father and son were used as a method, where one would be under the control of the HVO and the other one would go to no-man's land. Can you tell me who told you that and who were these people, the father and son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people were unknown to me, but I know, again, from their own stories, because one son came to the hospital seriously injured, and he was with me in the room. From his story, it was explained how he was wounded, how he got onto this line, and how they used this method, father/son. I can't say their names because I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You testified before the court in Mostar, the military tribunal. It was for the identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My guess is it was the military court, because this was a court that was inside a military facility, so it could be only military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that those people were tried for the murder of two Croats, not for the murder of Muslims, because Muslims could be killed freely. Why is it that you were called to identify those persons and to charge them with killing your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, these were not people, but one person, one man that was accused for the murder of our family. These people, we had to go and recognise, because they wanted to solve these cases that were still open. And this was a good opportunity, that there was one Croatian soldier who killed two Croatian soldiers, and because of that, they tried to pin it on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know what the Judges and the Prosecutors wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Judges -- first of all, I didn't have a lawyer. They told me, "Is this the man or not?" I said no, as it was the case, but the information that he killed two soldiers, I found that out from the soldiers who were taking care of me while my brother was testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know what the fate of that soldier was, whether he was acquitted for the murder of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that soldier. I think what I've heard is I was interested in it. When I visited Mostar during the summer, that together with him, there was one Muslim prisoner who was in the same cell, that he still remained in the prison cell afterwards. According to this Muslim prisoner, and what I have heard from him was this winter -- summer, summer, I think, when I returned to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So your conclusion that this trial was a travesty, that's what you said, and that it was just because of the international community. What do you base your conclusion on? What do you know about the trial, except for entering the courtroom and failing to recognise that person? What is it exactly that you know about that case that enables you to draw the conclusion that this was a travesty because of the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This trial was a farce because this man could not have committed all of the crimes he was accused of. His crimes were chosen really -- I don't know how he could have committed this crime. There were three people, how he could have done it on his own. Because there were three men in our case, and there was only one, it was only him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that person, that man, at that time was formally charged with the murder of your mother and brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived to testify. To recognise this man, if it was this man who committed that crime, that killing of our family, I didn't know. I don't know if he was accused of it, if he was indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were at the hospital just like Anna Frank, and you used that comparison very often, like Anna Frank in her house. You wanted to suggest that you were in hiding in that hospital. Can you please explain to me how it is that you were in hiding when the SIS colonel comes to your room, the police comes to your room, the Croatian soldier in the black uniform comes to your room? How is it that you were in hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to give you an example. For example, when these Muslim patients were taken away from the hospital, it was two or three times when a truck arrived to pick us up, the rest of us, the four of us, four patients that stayed there, they came again, so that's why we had to hide in the doctors' rooms so that they couldn't find us. Because if they had found us in the patients' room, they would have taken us. That's why we had to hide in the doctors' room. I used the example of Anna Frank so you could make a picture of what it was really like. I didn't want to compare it to Anna Frank, it was worse than that, because I saw personally eye into eye, this criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the last portion of your testimony, you said that patients were brought back to the Heliodrom, but that the last day, virtually, the whole hospital was cleansed, and that all the patients, even those who were on stretchers were taken to the Heliodrom. How do you know that these patients were taken to the Heliodrom and not to some other hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not taken to hospital because they were put rudely onto the truck because there would have been an ambulance and I don't know that people are taken by trucks to hospitals. And I know these people that were fatally wounded, they were returned from the Heliodrom to the hospital. That's how I know that they were at the Heliodrom, because not all the people, but maybe one-third that were seriously injured, that needed care, they came back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your father advised you before you were going to testify not to tell the truth. Now, what I want to know, after the first discussion, interview with the Prosecutor, did anyone advise you how to testify here and briefed you, trained you, coached you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody told me. Only as far as it was permitted, I was told how I would stand in front of this court, how I would solemnly declare that I would speak the truth, only that I gave my statement to the Prosecutor. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I did not mean the Prosecutor. I meant before you were approached by the Prosecution, I know that they are very correct in their behaviour, so somebody else outside of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who else could come. I could only share my experiences with my brother who experienced the same. I don't know who else, except my father, could give me advice what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who contacted you first about testifying after leaving Mostar in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the sense, we went to the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina who was responsible for making a list of those criminals. We cannot forget these criminals, and they have helped me a lot to present this case now in front of The Hague court, Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So did you give a statement to them? Did you talk to them, this section for war crimes at the BH embassy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of some benefits that I could get, that I could get my passport quicker, because all of those people whose lives were endangered, that they would have to spend several days in Zagreb, they were immediately given a passport to go to a third country. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you give your first statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Wednesday, last Wednesday, in my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you first get in touch with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Tuesday, last Tuesday. It could have been also Monday. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, two brief questions in closed session and we're done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will have a closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Becirovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I want to follow the whole --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I couldn't hear your question from the beginning. I couldn't hear the beginning of the question because there was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned that the soldiers came at your building to take you, and then they proceeded as you described to this horrible execution of your mother and brother. And you described them as HV soldiers, as Croatian. And that one of the signs was the accent, they had the accent of Split. Were they also dressed as HV soldiers or as HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed as HV soldiers. They had documents, badges, that can't be falsified, of HV military police. Among others, they also had the license plates that were yellow, and these were only HV license plates. Not knowing the city of Mostar showed that they came from the outside. According to their accent, I guessed that they were come from Dalmatia, Split, because there were a lot of soldiers from Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they were military police and they carried the insignia of HV. Were there many military police, HV military police, in the area or was it exceptional?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw for the first time military -- HV military police when they came at our door, but I saw before HV soldiers. I saw HV military police for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you say that they had a controlling attitude, that they were the masters of this situation, and obeyed around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When someone tells you what to do, that you should get dressed, that you should search on your own, of course, they were the masters of the situation. They could do with us whatever they wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not with you, not with you, with other soldiers. You said when you passed through the checkpoints, they were respected by the other soldiers. So they had a leading position; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could just see that they had no problems while passing those checkpoints. They didn't have to show any documents. They could move at that time. They were on their duty. They didn't use any kind of documents, so I concluded that they knew those policemen, those soldiers, at these checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke of what you called the cleansing of the hospital, was this cleansing done also by HV military police, by HV soldiers, if you remember rightly, or was it the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the force -- the HV forces -- it was the Fifth Brigade that was in the suburbs of Mostar, and the Fifth Brigade, I could recognise them by their truck because it said on the truck, "The Fifth Brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter has the question that I didn't understand clearly whether it was HV or HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think that's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think there's a clarification that the interpreter wanted that was just put on the record. If I may, I believe the interpreter, Judge Riad, with all due respect, I think the interpreter has some difficulty as I read the transcript and as I hear it, on either the answer or the question; I'm not sure which.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't understand whether the answer was HV or the HVO. The Fifth Battalion that was being mentioned, whether it was HV or HVO. It was not said clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you explain that? The Fifth Brigade, was it HV or HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifth HVO Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kehoe? Let me thank Judge Riad for having asked that question, which I myself wanted to ask. I want to really thank him because, in fact, since the very beginning of this testimony, there has been a great amount of confusion between HV, HVO, HV or HVO military police, HV or HVO troops. Therefore, I want to thank my colleague for having attempted to clarify all of these questions. Excuse me, Judge Shahabuddeen, because I interrupted you. Excuse me. You are now going to ask some questions, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You mentioned some soldiers who refused to fire at their erstwhile friends. Were they HV soldiers or HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were HVO soldiers since they were the only ones to have friends in Mostar. Because the HV, they come from the outside, they can't have friends in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
