utterances.text: Is my impression correct that from all that you have said, it appears that there were occasions when kindness was shown to you and surviving members of your family by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if they are your friends, of course they will show kindness to you. All of those crimes that were committed, they were not committed by my friends, that's for sure. Since we were not the kind of family to be on bad terms with anyone, to quarrel with people, we had a lot of friends and they all helped us. Among other things, I think that all the doctors in the Mostar hospital, they are the reason why we are still alive today, since my father and my mother, as a young couple, everybody knew them in Mostar, since they used to walk around together, everybody knew them in the street as a couple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would I be correct in supposing that these Croats who helped you and surviving members of your family knew that you were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not only did they know, they helped us, precisely because of that reason, because we were Muslim. They were the only ones in the position to help us. We needed any form of assistance we could get and, of course, they knew that we were Muslim. Everybody knew us. All those who knew us helped us, and that was the reason why the doctors helped us too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you help the Tribunal by telling us whether there were other cases in which Muslims were helped by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many cases of the neighbours who protected Muslims by hiding them in their homes when people came to collect them, it was the family Culjak, and other families, Doctors; we know a lot of such people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And what are your relations now with Croats who had proved to be helpful to you in your time of need?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, our relations are very good, just as they used to be before the war. Nothing's changed. They even proved themselves as true friends to us through providing assistance to us. All those people who helped us, we are very grateful to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sure that my colleague has one or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to add a question to the questions asked by my very eminent colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen. You are, apparently, a very educated, young student. Did you notice that the danger in which the Muslim population of Mostar, the danger which threatened them, was coming only from the military HVO or was the civilians, the Croat civilians, involved in this hatred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only did they threaten, but I learned that all the Muslims in Mostar, since they didn't like the fact that they existed in Mostar, they wanted to move them to Zenica. Zenica is a town in Central Bosnia which has a majority Muslim population. They wanted to move them all to Zenica. They had such plans. It doesn't mean that the plans were realised. They simply existed. That's what they were talking about amongst themselves, the Croats. That's how I heard it. But in Mostar, there was no room for Muslims. There was only room for Croats of Islamic faith, and that's a huge difference. The symbol of the city of Mostar, the old bridge, was destroyed by the Croatian Defence Council, because it was the symbol of Islam, and that was the foundation on which Mostar was built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished. I have no questions to add to those of my questions. Mr. Dragan Becirovic, everything you've experienced was very painful. You have many years of life ahead of you. As Judge Riad said, you are studying now, and you will one day be able to make further judgements about what has happened. You have a great mission in front of you, a great task. The Tribunal thanks you for having come to us at the request of the Prosecutor. The usher will now accompany you out of the courtroom. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Mr. Kehoe, this is the end of the afternoon. I would like to know how you see the rest of the week in light of what we said yesterday about the witnesses which you are supposed to call. We will finish at the end of the morning on Friday, as you know. What does the rest of the week look like, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a witness, the next witness that I informed counsel of. I don't mention his name simply because he's a protected witness, and then there is a possible next short witness after that which is the other individual that we previously discussed. And then we have a series of documents that my colleague, Mr. Cayley, will be discussing. That's tomorrow. We then have another witness that my colleague, Mr. Harmon, will be leading on Thursday, and I would suspect that that witness will go into Friday, but I will turn it over to Mr. Harmon, and I would think that he would be more available to answer that question accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we anticipate concluding on schedule, Friday, as previously indicated by the published schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to thank you, Mr. Harmon, for using your time properly. Of course, we're not counting every minute, but the days are counted, as you know, applying this measure rather broadly. I would also like you to think about the remainder of your work up to the end of July when you will have completed the presentation of your evidence. I believe that should be the 29th of July. I think that's right. Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUBUISSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have now only to thank the interpreters. I do it every day, but I particularly want to do it today, and so we will meet again tomorrow at 9.45, because the registrar asked us to begin at a quarter -- reasons of the detention facility and the arrival of the various accused. Thank you. Good evening, everybody. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.11 p.m. to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of July, 1998 at 9.45 a.m.
